fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, when I got to IIT Madras, I didn't go in thinking "I'm going to do AI." I think very few people did at that time. This was the late 2000s, so deep learning hadn't really taken off yet, and the department was much more oriented toward theory, algorithms, systems, that kind of thing. AI was almost a side interest.

What pulled me in was a couple of things. One was a course on, I think it was called knowledge representation and reasoning, and then later a machine learning course, and I remember being struck by how different the problems felt from the rest of computer science. Most of what we did had clean answers. You write a sorting algorithm, you prove it's correct, you're done. And here were these problems where the input was messy, like human language, or you were trying to get a system to learn something from examples, and there was no clean proof that it would work. It was more like science than engineering in that sense. You had to form hypotheses and run experiments and often be wrong.

The other thing was language specifically. I grew up in a multilingual environment, as most people in India do. You switch between Tamil and English and Hindi within a single sentence sometimes, and so the question of how a machine could possibly deal with that felt both very personal and very hard. I did a small project on something like text classification for Indian languages, nothing fancy, but I remember just how badly the standard tools worked and thinking, okay, there's clearly a lot of room here.

And then I'd say the environment mattered. IIT Madras had this culture where the professors were very approachable, you could just walk into someone's office and say I want to work on this, and they'd hand you papers and say come back in two weeks. There weren't a lot of resources compared to a place like MIT, no big GPU clusters or anything, but that constraint was almost useful. You had to think carefully about what experiment was worth running. I think that shaped how I approach research even now.

opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, when I got to IIT Madras I wasn't set on AI. I came in with a general love for computer science: algorithms, systems, the satisfaction of making a machine do exactly what you specify. What pulled me toward AI was the realization that there was a whole class of problems where you *couldn't* specify exactly what you wanted. Understanding a sentence, recognizing what's in an image, making a decision under uncertainty. You can't write down a clean set of rules for those, and that felt both frustrating and fascinating.

Language especially grabbed me. As humans we take it for granted. We read a paragraph and just get it. But when you try to get a computer to do that, you see how much hidden structure, ambiguity and world knowledge are packed into even simple text. That gap between how effortless it is for us and how hard it is for machines seemed like one of the most interesting puzzles you could work on.

The environment mattered too. You were surrounded by very sharp peers, and there was a culture of tinkering, of trying projects beyond the coursework. Getting my hands dirty on a few research-style problems as an undergrad showed me that this wasn't just an abstract field. You could build something, watch it fail in interesting ways, and learn from that. That loop of trying ideas, seeing what the model gets wrong and iterating is what hooked me, and it's really what led me to grad school at MIT and to working on language and learning more seriously.

At the time, of course, AI wasn't the giant thing it is today. It felt like a fairly niche, almost speculative area. Part of the appeal was precisely that: it felt like a lot was still unknown, and there was room to contribute something meaningful.

fable-5.text:
Thanks for having me. So, to be honest, when I started at IIT Madras, AI wasn't really the plan — I went in like most students there just wanting to do computer science broadly. But somewhere in my second or third year, I took a course on artificial intelligence, and what really hooked me was language. I was always fascinated by the fact that we as humans communicate with this incredibly rich, ambiguous medium, and yet somehow we understand each other most of the time. The idea that you could get a machine to do even a fraction of that felt like one of the hardest and most interesting problems out there.

This was also before the deep learning wave had really taken off, so a lot of what we were doing involved more classical techniques — logic, search, statistical methods. And in some ways that was a blessing, because it forced you to think carefully about the structure of the problem rather than just throwing data at it. India also has this interesting linguistic landscape — dozens of languages, people code-switching constantly — so the challenges of language technology felt very tangible, not abstract. You could see directly how much it would matter if machines could actually handle language well.

I also got lucky with mentorship. I had professors who encouraged me to do research as an undergrad, work on small projects, read papers, and that gave me a taste of what it was like to push on an open problem rather than just solve assignments. By the time I graduated, it was pretty clear to me that I wanted to pursue natural language processing seriously, which is what took me to grad school and eventually down the path that led to everything after.

opus-5.text:
Honestly, it wasn't like I showed up with a plan. When I got there, AI wasn't the thing everyone was clamoring to do — a lot of my batchmates were headed toward systems, or finance, or just straight to industry. I think I stumbled into it through a couple of courses. There was an NLP course, and the thing that struck me was that it was the first time in my CS education where the problem didn't have a clean specification. Everything else I'd learned was, here's the spec, write the program, prove it terminates. And suddenly you're dealing with language, where nobody can even write down what the right answer is.

That really got under my skin. The idea that you could have a system learn the rules from data instead of you sitting there hand-coding every case — at the time that felt almost like cheating, in a good way.

The other part was the people. IIT Madras had a pretty strong group working on speech and language, and as an undergrad you could actually go knock on a professor's door and end up on a project. I spent a lot of time in those labs doing things that didn't work, which in hindsight was the most useful education I got there.

sonnet-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. Honestly, when I got to IIT Madras I wasn't sure AI was what I wanted to do. I knew I liked computer science, and I liked the idea of building things that could do something useful. But AI was still a pretty niche area then, and a lot of what we studied was classical: search, logic, probabilistic models, and early machine learning.

What pulled me in was how open-ended the questions felt. In most areas of CS, you can more or less define the problem and then work out the most efficient way to solve it. In AI, you're often trying to figure out what the problem even is. What does it mean for a machine to understand a sentence? How do you get a system to make good decisions when it doesn't have all the information? Those questions felt like they sat somewhere between engineering and something more philosophical, and I found that really compelling.

Language in particular fascinated me. We use it so effortlessly, but when you try to get a computer to do the same thing, you realize how much is going on underneath. Ambiguity, context, and common sense all matter. I think that mix of being very hard and very human is what kept me hooked, and it's what eventually led me to focus on language and learning.
